title: Sikhism: remembering the name
hook: remembering God through the name, in breath and song

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ik Onkar, the numeral one that opens the Sikh scripture. Your line was one.

Long before sunrise in Amritsar, the city is dark, but the Golden Temple is lit up, its reflection shivering on the water around it. People are already walking the marble path barefoot, and from inside comes music: a harmonium, small drums, voices singing verses from the scripture. It goes on, in shifts, almost all day. Some of the walkers sing along. Some are silent, lips barely moving, repeating a single word.
screen: `BEFORE SUNRISE IN AMRITSAR.` → `MUSIC FROM INSIDE THE TEMPLE.` → `ONE WORD, LIPS BARELY MOVING.`

segments.voice: Naam means the name. In Sikh teaching it's more than a label: it's the presence of the one creator, yesterday's Ik Onkar, running through everything. Simran means remembering. So naam simran is remembering the name, keeping the one close until the mind is steeped in it. Sikh tradition counts it the first of three pillars of Sikh life, taught by Guru Nanak; the other two, honest work and sharing, come in the next two days. How is it done? Sikhs often repeat Waheguru, a Sikh name for God often explained as wonderful Lord, or wondrous teacher, silently or aloud, sometimes with the breath: wahe on the in-breath, guru on the out-breath. Some rise in the hours before dawn, called amrit vela, the ambrosial time, to bathe, recite Japji and sit in simran before the day starts. And much of it is sung. The Guru Granth Sahib is written almost entirely as poetry set to musical modes called raags, and kirtan, singing it, fills the gurdwara. A line in the Sukhmani Sahib, by the fifth Guru, Arjan, says in effect: remember, remember, remember, and find peace. The Gurus taught this wasn't escape from the world. Guru Nanak compared a person living with the name to a lotus that grows in muddy water yet isn't stained by it. The idea is to keep the name while living a full, busy life, not instead of one.
screen: `NAAM — THE NAME, THE PRESENCE.` · `SIMRAN — REMEMBERING.` · `WAHEGURU, WITH THE BREATH.` · `A LOTUS IN MUDDY WATER.` · then, large: `THE NAME.`

segments.voice: Borrowed from kirtan: breathe in, and on the out-breath let one low, easy note hum in your chest. If you're Sikh, you might let Waheguru ride on the note; if not, the hum alone is enough, or any word that points you toward what matters. When thoughts come, let them float like the lotus on the water, and come back to the sound.
Naam simran. Remembering the name: keeping the one creator in mind, in breath and song, through a busy day. Today's word.
Your line: the name. In breath, in song, in the hours before dawn. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs rise at amrit vela before dawn to recite Japji and meditate on Waheguru, join kirtan in the gurdwara, and repeat the name quietly through the day.

notes: Review 2026-10-01: hook no longer opens 'It's three in the morning' (day 269 opened 'two in the morning'); practice changed from repeating one word on the breath (done on days 267 and 269) to a hummed note from kirtan; cut the Sanskrit-root etymology, 'famous', and 'many Sikhs'.
Sukhmani Sahib, Ang 262: 'simar simar simar sukh paavau' paraphrased as 'remember, remember, remember, and find peace'. Confirm Ang and sense.
Lotus image: several places in Gurbani (e.g. Sidh Gosht, Ang 938); confirm the reference.
Waheguru breathing (wahe in, guru out) is a common practice, not universal.
Three pillars (naam japna, kirat karni, vand chhakna) are traditional; the script uses naam simran for the first per the index.
